# Love, on Two Wheels

Today, I want to tell a story about love. I know you are probably thinking I am going to tell you about my love life. Well Sorry to disappoint you but this is a story about my father. 

Growing up my father owned a motorcycle. He still does. To most people, it was simply a motorcycle. To me, it was the sound of safety, it was a sign that my friend was around the corner.

Whenever I heard its familiar engine approaching our home, I would dash outside before it even came to a complete stop. I couldn't wait to tell my father about every injustice I had suffered that day in the hands of my other family member — who had teased me, who had been unkind, who had made me cry. He would climb off the motorcycle, pull me into a hug, and say the words that instantly made everything feel okay:

> *"Nitachapa hao watu."*

Loosely translated to, "I'll deal with them."

I don't think he ever actually intended to fight anyone. But as a little girl, I believed him. Those words made me feel protected. They reminded me that no matter what had happened during the day, someone was always on my side. I even used to tell other kids at school 'My Father will beat you plus your whole household', well he used to be a boxer in his prime, so I knew what I was talking about.

Looking back, I realize that sometimes love sounds like reassurance.

## Our Family Vehicle


For many years, that motorcycle was our family vehicle.  Eventually, my father even turned it into a source of income. But before it became a business, it carried our family through countless ordinary moments that would later become extraordinary memories. It took me to school every morning and brought me home every evening. It carried us through seasons of joy and seasons of uncertainty.

## A Memory That Remains Vivid

During the 2007 post-election violence, roads that had once been familiar suddenly became dangerous. Fires burned along our usual route, and protests made travel unpredictable. Yet somehow, my father found a way to get me home safely. He navigated unfamiliar roads, taking long detours until we finally reached home. At the time, I didn't fully understand what was happening around me. Now I do. That motorcycle didn't just carry us — it carried me to safety.

## Fries, a Soda, and Quality Time

![][image_ref_46weurvd]

One day, my father invited me to accompany him to his farm in Homa Bay County. I was thrilled, because i'd get to escape house chores. As a child, I admired how hardworking he was, and spending the day with him felt like the greatest adventure.

We arrived early at the farm and walked around the farm while he worked. I mostly watched, asked questions, and followed him from one corner of the shamba to another. After a long day in the shamba we decided to head home before the afternoon rains start. Before heading home, we stopped at Dhiwa Resort for fries and a soda — my favourite meal at the time. To anyone else, it was just fries and a soft drink. To me, it was quality time with my father.

When I got home, I proudly narrated every detail of our adventure to my siblings, I am convinced they were secretly jealous of my special day.


## The Science Assignment
![][image_ref_xapquxea]

Then there was the science assignment. My teacher had asked us to collect different types of weeds and paste them into our science books. While many of my classmates searched around their homes, my father turned it into another adventure.

We rode from village to village as he pointed out plants he knew by name. Together, we collected far more varieties than I ever expected.

When I earned an A on that assignment, it felt like my achievement. Today, I realize it was ours.

He gave up his time, his energy, and an entire afternoon simply to help his daughter succeed.

That, too, was love.


## Full Circle
![][image_ref_7aqheewd]
This afternoon, while walking to the supermarket, I saw a father riding a motorcycle with his young daughter seated behind him.

For a brief moment, I wasn't an adult anymore.

I was that little girl again, waiting by the gate, listening for the sound of my father's motorcycle.

It reminded me that love isn't always expressed through grand speeches or expensive gifts.

Sometimes love is a ride to school.

Sometimes it's taking the long way home to keep your child safe.

Sometimes it's spending an entire day helping collect weeds for a science project.

Sometimes it's fries and a soda after a day at the farm.

And sometimes, love sounds like a father saying,

*"Nitachapa hao watu."* even when i am the stubborn child.

As children, we rarely notice these moments because they feel ordinary. Our brain teaches us to focus on the wrong things that happened. The ones that made you almost pack your bags and escape from home only to come back because you dont have bus fare.

As adults, we realize they were never ordinary at all.
